passage:
On Monday Rajni's mother came home and let out a long sigh as she dropped her bag. Jasleen, sitting at her homework, felt her stomach drop. Did I do something? She stopped writing.

On Tuesday it happened again, and this time Jasleen asked, “Amma, is everything fine?”

Her mother blinked. “Oh, beta, the bus was packed and my feet hurt. That sigh was just tiredness.” She smiled. On Thursday Rajni's mother sighed again, dropped into the sofa and laughed, “That was relief. The report is finished!” Jasleen giggled and put her pencil back on the page.

qa.q: On which day did Rajni's mother explain that her sigh was tiredness?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Jasleen think when she heard her mother's first sigh, and why?
qa.a: She worried she had done something wrong, because she read the sigh as annoyance directed at her.

qa.q: What worked better than guessing, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether everything was fine, since the sighs turned out to be tiredness and relief and not anger at her.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother feel when she learns Jasleen worried about her sighs?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and want to be clearer, since she never meant the sighs to be about Jasleen.

grounding: A schoolchild reads an adult's sigh as annoyance, then learns by asking that it was tiredness and relief.

passage: Aparna, my granddaughter, you asked why I always ask people, “Everything fine?” when they sigh. Let me tell you. When I was eleven, our teacher, Mr. Iyer, sighed loudly every time I read aloud. I decided I was a terrible reader and stopped putting my hand up. For a whole term I sat quiet. Years later I met him, an old man, and told him. He looked amazed. “Rukmini, I had a bad back that year! I sighed whenever I stood up.” I laughed and cried together. So now I ask. A sigh can be tired, bored, cross or glad, and I don't want any child to blame herself.

qa.q: How old was Rukmini when Mr. Iyer sighed at Rukmini's reading?
qa.a: Rukmini was eleven.

qa.q: Why did young Rukmini stop putting her hand up in class?
qa.a: Young Rukmini took the sighs to mean being a terrible reader, so felt discouraged and hid.

qa.q: What could a child do when a grown-up's sigh worries them?
qa.a: A child could ask something like “Is everything fine?” and not assume being the cause.

qa.q: How might Mr. Iyer have felt when he found out what Rukmini believed?
qa.a: He was amazed and probably sorry, because his sighs came from a bad back and had nothing to do with Rukmini's reading.

grounding: An elder recounts how a child read a teacher's sigh as annoyance, though it was tiredness, showing the ambiguity and value of asking.

passage: The clinic's waiting room was packed, the token number hadn't moved in an hour, and Nilesh's wrist throbbed in its sling. Beside him, his father, Chetan, let out a long, heavy sigh. Nilesh shrank. He's annoyed with me. I shouldn't have jumped off the wall. Another sigh, longer. Nilesh couldn't bear it. “Papa, are you angry I got hurt?” Chetan turned, surprised. “Angry? No. I was sighing because the doctor's message just came: the X-ray shows only a sprain, not a break.” He held up his phone. “That was a relief sigh. Two of them.” Nilesh let out his own breath. “I thought it was me.”

qa.q: What did the X-ray show?
qa.a: The X-ray showed only a sprain, not a break.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when his father sighed?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty and worried, sure his father was annoyed with him for jumping off the wall.

qa.q: What did asking achieve?
qa.a: It showed the sighs were relief about the X-ray, so Nilesh stopped blaming himself.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan was worried about the wrist and tired of waiting, and then relieved when the X-ray message came.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's sigh as annoyance at him, and asking to learn it was relief.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Pradeep brought his model volcano to the table where Amma was working. “Amma, can you help me with the lava?” Kalyani stared at her laptop and huffed, a short, sharp breath through her nose. Pradeep stepped back. She's fed up with me. I always ask at the wrong time. He turned to go. Then he stopped and asked, “Is that huff about me?” Kalyani looked up, surprised, then rubbed her eyes. “Oh, kanna, no. The internet just cut out in the middle of my meeting. For the third time.” She closed the laptop. “Ten minutes of lava. Then I'll try again.”

qa.q: What was Pradeep's model?
qa.a: Pradeep's model was a volcano.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when Kalyani huffed?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and unwanted, thinking she was fed up with him for asking at the wrong time.

qa.q: Why was it good that Pradeep asked about the huff?
qa.a: Asking showed the huff was about the internet cutting out, so he didn't walk away blaming himself.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Kalyani?
qa.a: Kalyani was frustrated by the internet cutting out three times during her meeting.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's huff as annoyance with him, and asking to find a different cause.

passage: Nazia finished the last bar of the piece and looked up. Maria Miss let out a long sigh and closed her eyes. “Was it that bad?” Nazia asked, voice small. “Bad?” Maria Miss opened her eyes. “Why do you say that?” “You sighed. Like my brother does when I'm annoying.” “Ah.” She laughed. “No. That was a happy sigh. You finally played the tricky bit without stopping. I've been waiting three weeks to hear that.” “Oh.” Nazia's shoulders dropped. “I thought you were tired of me.” “Tired, maybe. It's my sixth lesson today. But never of you.” Nazia grinned and played it again.

qa.q: How long had Maria Miss been waiting to hear the tricky bit?
qa.a: She had been waiting three weeks.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Maria Miss sighed?
qa.a: Nazia felt anxious and small, fearing the sigh meant the playing was bad or that Nazia was annoying.

qa.q: What did Nazia's question make possible?
qa.a: It let Maria Miss explain the sigh was happy relief, so Nazia stopped assuming Nazia was the problem.

qa.q: What did the sigh mean for Maria Miss?
qa.a: For Maria Miss it was a happy, tired sigh of relief that the tricky bit had finally been played right 🎶

grounding: Shows a child reading an adult's sigh as annoyance, when it was relief and tiredness, and asking before assuming.

passage:
The summer I stayed with Ayesha Khala in Bhopal, I was sure I was annoying her. Every evening she would sit down after work and let out a long "Haaaah." I'd freeze, then quietly tidy something, or go and read in the other room.

One night, after one of those huge sighs, I finally asked, "Khala, is everything fine? Did I do something?"

She looked at me, surprised, then pulled me onto the sofa. "You? That sigh means my feet have stopped moving at last! It's my happy sigh."

I'm Sabina, and I still remember how much lighter I felt. Now when someone sighs near me, I ask before I start tidying.

qa.q: Where did Sabina stay that summer?
qa.a: With Ayesha Khala in Bhopal.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel each time Ayesha Khala let out a long sigh?
qa.a: Anxious and worried about being the cause of her annoyance, so Sabina froze and went quietly to tidy or read elsewhere.

qa.q: What did Sabina learn to do when someone sighs?
qa.a: Ask before assuming, just as Sabina finally did with "Is everything fine? Did I do something?"

qa.q: What did Ayesha Khala's sigh actually mean?
qa.a: Relief and contentment that her feet could rest after work; she was surprised that it had been read as annoyance.

grounding: It is a child's look back at reading an adult's evening sigh as annoyance at them, and learning by asking that it was relief.
